content: The document titled Recommendations and Guidance on Hepatitis C Virus Self-Testing was published in July 2021 by the World Health Organization (WHO). It provides evidence from multiple countries on the usability and acceptability of self-testing for hepatitis C virus (HCV). The publication is authored by Elena Ivanova Reipold, Thi Thuy Van Nguyen, Gamal Shihah, Ketevan Stvilia, Aliza Monroe-Wise, Cheng Wang, Muhammad S. Jamil, Cheryl C. Johnson, and Philippa Easterbrook, among others. The publication is part of WHO's guidelines on hepatitis C virus self-testing and is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes. It aligns with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014). The background section highlights that globally, less than 20% of individuals with HCV infection have been tested, and only a quarter of those diagnosed have received treatment. Self-testing for HCV antibodies (HCVST) is proposed as an additional strategy to increase access to testing and support elimination efforts. Studies were conducted to evaluate the usability and acceptability of HCVST among the general population and key populations, including men who have sex with men (MSM) and people who inject drugs (PWID). The methods section describes observational studies conducted in five countries: Egypt (general population), China (MSM), Kenya (PWID), and Vietnam and Georgia (PWID and MSM). The OraQuick® HCV Rapid Antibody Test, adapted for self-testing, was used as a prototype. Participants were provided with written and pictorial instructions for use (IFU) and conducted the self-test in a private room under the observation of a trained individual. In Egypt, participants also received one-on-one demonstrations. Usability was assessed through observer evaluations of errors and difficulties using a standardized checklist, while acceptability was measured using semi-structured questionnaires. Participants interpreted their test results, which were then re-read by the observer. All participants were re-tested using a professional OraQuick® HCV test performed by a trained provider. The results section reports that 775 participants were enrolled across the five studies. The highest proportion of participants completing all testing steps without errors was observed in Egypt and Georgia (>70%), while the lowest was among PWID in Kenya (30%) and Vietnam (46%). The most common error was incorrect sample collection. Inter-reader agreement ranged from 86% to 99%, and inter-operator agreement ranged from 85% to 99%. A majority of PWID in Vietnam and Kenya required assistance with self-testing. The proportion of participants who found the kit easy or very easy to use ranged from 55% in Egypt and 66% in Kenya to over 80% in other countries. Acceptability was high, with over 90% of participants in four countries willing to use HCVST again and recommend it to family and friends. The conclusion states that these are the first global studies to demonstrate high usability and acceptability of HCVST among both general and key populations. While most users were able to self-test with ease, assisted self-testing models are necessary for certain populations, such as PWID. HCVST is identified as a promising tool for increasing testing coverage and achieving elimination goals. The abstract of this work was previously presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Boston in March 2021.
